phrases.text: Okay, let's get started.
You all read The Necklace by Guy de Maupassant last night.
I want to start with Mathilde.
What did you think of her as a character, and what in the text makes you think that?
I honestly think she's really selfish.
From the very first page she's unhappy with everything she has, even though her husband is trying really hard for her.
He gives up the money he was saving for a gun so she can buy a dress, and she still complains that she doesn't have any jewelry.
So I think the whole story is about how her greed ruins her life, because if she had just been happy with what she had, none of this would have happened.
She's just annoying.
She's the worst character in the story.
Leo, what makes her the worst?
Can you point to something?
She just is.
She cries about everything.
Her husband is way better.
I want to build on what Jonah said about the husband giving up his savings.
I agree she's selfish there, but I think the story also shows she doesn't have anywhere to put those feelings.
The narrator says she was born into a family of clerks, almost by mistake, so it's like she feels trapped in the wrong life.
Yeah, but lots of people feel trapped and they don't act like that.
She borrows the necklace, she loses it, and then instead of telling the truth she hides it from her friend for ten years.
That's a choice.
Nobody forced her to lie.
So I still think it's mostly on her, because the lie is what actually costs them everything.
So we have two readings: she's selfish, or she's trapped.
Does anyone see it differently?
I think she's selfish.
Jonah's right.
And the husband is kind of the opposite.
He's happy with soup for dinner, he says there's nothing better than a good stew.
He's content with simple things.
So I think Maupassant puts them side by side on purpose, to make her look worse.
It's a classic contrast.
That's a good point about the contrast.
But if Maupassant wanted us to just hate her, why does he spend so much time inside her head, describing her dreams about quiet rooms and tapestries?
It makes me feel sorry for her, at least a little.
So maybe he wants us to understand her, not only judge her.
Interesting.
Maya's asking why the narrator spends so much time in her head.
Let's hold that.
Priya, you've been listening.
What are you thinking?
I'm not sure yet.
I kind of agree with Maya.
That's fine.
Let's move to the ending.
When Madame Forestier says the necklace was fake, worth five hundred francs at most, how did you react?
I thought it was a great twist.
The whole time you think the tragedy is losing the necklace, and then it turns out the ten years were for nothing.
It's ironic because she wanted to look rich, and the thing that made her look rich was fake the whole time.
So the story is basically saying appearances are fake, and if you chase them, you lose real things.
The ending is unfair.
It's a bad ending.
Unfair to whom, Leo?
To her.
And to the reader.
It's just unfair.
I sort of see what Leo means.
Building on that, it feels unfair because she actually changed.
She works for ten years, she learns what being poor really is, and the story says she became strong and hard.
So she grows, and then the ending takes that away from her in one sentence.
Maybe that's why it feels unfair.
But I don't think she really grew.
She still goes up to Madame Forestier at the end almost to show off that she paid it back.
She's proud of it.
So it's still about how other people see her.
For example, she smiles with a proud and simple joy.
That's still pride.
Jonah's pointing at that proud joy.
What do others make of it?
I think it can be both.
She's proud, but maybe she's proud of something real for the first time, the work, not the dress.
I agree with Jonah that it's pride, but I disagree that it's the same pride as the beginning.
Okay, that's fair, but the story doesn't show us that she sees it that way.
We never hear her think the work was valuable.
We only see what she lost, like her looks.
The narrator says she looked old now.
So I think the focus is still on appearances, even at the end.
Let's widen out.
What do you think the story is saying about money and class more broadly?
I think it's saying the class system makes people want things they can't have.
The ball is full of rich people, and for one night she gets to be one of them, and everybody admires her.
That one night is basically what destroys her.
So the story is criticizing a society where your worth is how you look.
Rich people are fake.
That's what it's saying.
Leo, what in the story shows that rich people are fake?
The necklace.
It was fake.
Actually that connects to what Leo said.
Madame Forestier is rich and her necklace is fake, but nobody can tell.
So maybe the point is that you can't tell who's rich just by looking, which means what Mathilde wanted was never really real in the first place.
Right, and that goes with what I said about appearances.
Also, the ball is the only time she's happy in the whole story, and it's all based on something borrowed.
Her happiness is borrowed.
I think that's the main message.
Before we wrap up, I want to make sure we hear from everyone.
Priya, anything you've been thinking about?
Yeah.
If Mathilde had just told Madame Forestier the truth that night, she would have found out the necklace was fake.
So is the story saying the real tragedy wasn't losing the necklace, but being too ashamed to admit it?
Why does Maupassant make her pride the thing that costs her, instead of bad luck?
That's a really important question.
Who wants to take it on?
I think Priya's right that it's the shame, not the loss.
Losing it was bad luck, but hiding it was a choice.
Building on Priya's question, the story could have been about bad luck, but because the lie is what costs ten years, it has to be about pride.
Yeah, I agree with Priya.
That's actually what I was saying earlier about the lie being a choice.
If she had been honest, the whole ten years disappears.
So the story punishes dishonesty more than greed.
So it's about lying.
Lying is bad.
Leo, can you say more?
Why would Maupassant care about lying more than wanting things?
I don't know.
It's just the moral.
Maybe because wanting things is normal, but she lets it decide what she does?
Oh, I like that.
So the wanting isn't the problem, it's letting other people's opinion decide what you do.
Like when she couldn't face telling her friend.
That also explains the husband.
He goes along with the lie too, so it's not just her.
He signs all those loans.
So both of them care what Madame Forestier thinks.
Maybe the story is about how everyone in that society is trapped by what other people think, not just Mathilde.
So we've moved from Mathilde is selfish to the whole society.
That's a big shift.
Last quick thoughts: has anyone's view of Mathilde changed today?
Mine has.
I started thinking she was just shallow, but now I think she's more of an example of what the society does to people.
I still think she's responsible for her choices, but I see the society part more now, especially after Priya's question.
Great discussion.
For tomorrow, write a paragraph answering Priya's question, using at least two quotes from the story.
